claim: MorphoGraphX is an open-source software platform for quantifying morphogenesis in 4D.
source: Here we present a method and the open-source software MorphoGraphX (www.MorphoGraphX.org, Box 1) to quantify the temporal evolution of cellular geometry and fluorescence signal on curved 2D surface layers of cells over multiple time points in both plants and animals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that MorphoGraphX is open-source software designed for quantifying morphogenesis.

claim: MorphoGraphX can process curved surface images extracted from 3D data.
source: Here we present MorphoGraphX (www.MorphoGraphX.org), a software that bridges this gap by working directly with curved surface images extracted from 3D data.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this capability of the software.

claim: MorphoGraphX includes algorithms for cell segmentation on curved surfaces.
source: In addition to traditional 3D image analysis, we have developed algorithms to operate on curved surfaces, such as cell segmentation, lineage tracking and fluorescence signal quantification.
evidence: The abstract lists cell segmentation as one of the algorithms developed for curved surfaces.

claim: MorphoGraphX includes algorithms for lineage tracking on curved surfaces.
source: In addition to traditional 3D image analysis, we have developed algorithms to operate on curved surfaces, such as cell segmentation, lineage tracking and fluorescence signal quantification.
evidence: The abstract lists lineage tracking as one of the algorithms developed for curved surfaces.

claim: MorphoGraphX includes algorithms for fluorescence signal quantification on curved surfaces.
source: In addition to traditional 3D image analysis, we have developed algorithms to operate on curved surfaces, such as cell segmentation, lineage tracking and fluorescence signal quantification.
evidence: The abstract lists fluorescence signal quantification as one of the algorithms developed for curved surfaces.

claim: Cell geometries extracted with MorphoGraphX can be exported and used as templates for simulation models.
source: Cell geometries extracted with MorphoGraphX can be exported and used as templates for simulation models, providing a powerful platform to investigate the interactions between shape, genes and growth.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this capability.

claim: Morphogenesis emerges from complex multiscale interactions between genetic and mechanical processes.
source: Morphogenesis emerges from complex multiscale interactions between genetic and mechanical processes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: Computer simulations are becoming widely used to study morphogenesis due to the complexity of temporal and spatial interactions involved.
source: Because of the complexity of temporal and spatial interactions involved, computer simulations are becoming widely used (Dumais and Steele, 2000; Jönsson et al., 2006; Sick et al., 2006; Lecuit and Lenne, 2007; Merks et al., 2007; Stoma et al., 2008; Kondo and Miura, 2010; Varner et al., 2010; Kennaway et al., 2011; Santuari et al., 2011; Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012; Kierzkowski et al., 2012; Bassel et al., 2014; Milde et al., 2014; Sampathkumar et al., 2014; Yoshida et al., 2014) in what is now being called Computational Morphodynamics (Chickarmane et al., 2010).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Confocal microscopy is frequently the tool of choice for data collection in morphogenesis studies.
source: Confocal microscopy is frequently the tool of choice for data collection, as the proliferation of fluorescence markers and variations in the method make it possible to visualize proteins, organelles, cell boundaries, and even protein–protein interaction and protein movement in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about the field.

claim: Serial block-face scanning electron microscopy makes it possible to study sub-cellular structures at higher resolution than confocal microscopy on fixed samples.
source: Other technologies such as serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Denk and Horstmann, 2004) make it possible to study sub-cellular structures at a much higher resolution on fixed samples.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: There is a lack of methods and software to process and quantify 3D imaging data and integrate them within simulation environments.
source: However, despite the rapid advancement of 3D imaging technologies, there is a lack of methods and software to process and quantify these data and to integrate them within simulation environments.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for developing MorphoGraphX.

claim: Most simulation models of morphogenesis operate on 2D templates.
source: Most simulation models of morphogenesis operate on 2D templates (Dumais and Steele, 2000; Jönsson et al., 2006; Sick et al., 2006; Merks et al., 2007; Stoma et al., 2008; Kondo and Miura, 2010; Varner et al., 2010; Kennaway et al., 2011; Santuari et al., 2011; Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012; Kierzkowski et al., 2012; Sampathkumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published models.

claim: Many key biological processes occur on surfaces, for example in epithelial layers.
source: This is not surprising since many key biological processes occur on surfaces, for example in epithelial layers (Lecuit and Lenne, 2007; Savaldi-Goldstein et al., 2007; Heller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Morphogenesis involves complex 3D deformation, such as folding during gastrulation in animal systems or bulging out of new lateral organs in plants.
source: Morphogenesis involves complex 3D deformation, such as folding during gastrulation in animal systems or bulging out of new lateral organs in plants, causing significant curvature in the tissues controlling these events.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about morphogenesis.

claim: The simplest method to quantify cell shapes on curved surfaces is to take several image slices and project them onto a single plane.
source: The simplest method to achieve this is to take several image slices and project them onto a single plane (Butler et al., 2009; Chickarmane et al., 2010; Kuchen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published methods.

claim: Distortions due to flat projection become too large as the angle between the surface and the projection plane increases.
source: However, when trying to quantify cell shape change, division orientations, or growth, distortions due to the projection quickly become too large as the angle between the surface and the projection plane increases.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of flat projection methods.

claim: Even small amounts of tissue curvature can hinder the accurate imaging of a single cell layer over an entire sample.
source: Even small amounts of tissue curvature can hinder the accurate imaging of a single cell layer over an entire sample.
evidence: This is stated as a problem with existing methods.

claim: Methods have been developed to determine the 3D position of cell junctions on the surface while segmentation is performed on flat 2D images.
source: To alleviate some of these issues, methods have been developed to determine the 3D position of cell junctions on the surface, while the segmentation into cells is still performed on flat 2D images (Dumais and Kwiatkowska, 2002; de Reuille et al., 2005; Routier-Kierzkowska and Kwiatkowska, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published methods.

claim: Methods based on tissue casts combined with stereo reconstruction of SEM images are labor intensive and limited to tissues that can be visualized as a flat 2D image.
source: However these approaches are labor intensive, limited to tissues that can be visualized as a flat 2D image, and are not accurate when the angle of the tissue with the projection plane becomes too large.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: Methods based on tissue casts combined with stereo reconstruction of SEM images need to be combined with methods using fluorescent markers if gene expression is to be monitored.
source: Furthermore, methods based on tissue casts combined with stereo reconstruction of SEM images (Dumais and Kwiatkowska, 2002; Routier-Kierzkowska and Kwiatkowska, 2008) need to be combined with methods using fluorescent markers (Uyttewaal et al., 2012) if gene expression is to be monitored.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: MorphoGraphX can render full 3D volumetric data from Confocal Laser Scanning Microscopy, Magnetic Resonance Imaging and block-face SEM.
source: Modern imaging technologies today provide us with an abundance of data from a variety of sources: Confocal Laser Scanning Microscopy, Magnetic Resonance Imaging and block-face SEM all provide full 3D volumetric data that can be rendered in MorphoGraphX (Figure 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: MorphoGraphX can process surfaces imported from 3D scanners, reconstructions from Stereo-SEM images, focus stacking microscopes and scanning probe methods such as Cellular Force Microscopy.
source: Our software can also process surfaces, which can be imported from 3D scanners, reconstructions from Stereo-SEM images (Routier-Kierzkowska and Kwiatkowska, 2008), focus stacking microscopes and scanning probe methods such as Cellular Force Microscopy (Routier-Kierzkowska et al., 2012) (CFM), or extracted within MorphoGraphX from full 3D data sets (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: MorphoGraphX contains a highly optimized rendering engine capable of accurate rendering of both semi-transparent surfaces and volumetric data simultaneously.
source: MorphoGraphX contains a highly optimized rendering engine that is capable of accurate rendering of both semi-transparent surfaces and volumetric data simultaneously.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the software.

claim: Surfaces in MorphoGraphX are represented by an oriented triangular mesh.
source: Surfaces are represented by an oriented triangular mesh, which is typically extracted from the surface of an object, and thus represents the outermost tissue layer (Figure 1A,C,D), or the boundaries of individual 3D objects (e.g., cells) in the case of full 3D segmentation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Surfaces and associated data from MorphoGraphX can be exported in a variety of file formats suitable for loading into modeling or analysis softwares.
source: Once processed, surfaces and associated data can be exported in a variety of file formats suitable for loading into modeling or analysis softwares, allowing the direct use of sample geometry in computer simulations (Santuari et al., 2011; Kierzkowski et al., 2012; Bassel et al., 2014; Sampathkumar et al., 2014; Yoshida et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work that used this capability.

claim: MorphoGraphX can create a curved image of the outer layer of cells by projecting 3D data just below the surface onto the extracted organ shape.
source: After extracting the shape of an organ, 3D data just below the surface can be projected onto it, creating a curved image of the outer layer of cells (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: Curved surface projection in MorphoGraphX enables the extraction of precise cell outlines without the distortions associated with a flat 2D projection.
source: This enables the extraction of precise cell outlines without the distortions associated with a flat 2D projection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many algorithms designed for 2 and 3D image processing can be adapted to curved surface images in MorphoGraphX.
source: We have found that many algorithms designed for 2 and 3D image processing can be adapted to our curved surface images.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the software development.

claim: Feature extraction in MorphoGraphX typically follows a pattern: volumetric data is pre-processed, the object of interest is turned into a mask, the object is extracted as a surface mesh, volumetric data is projected onto the surface, and the projection is used for segmentation.
source: Feature extraction in MorphoGraphX typically follows a pattern: (i) volumetric data (often a cell outline marker) is pre-processed to remove noise or obstructions; (ii) the object of interest is turned into a mask (binary image); (iii) the object is extracted as a surface mesh; (iv) volumetric data is projected onto the surface; (v) the projection is used for segmentation of the surface into cells (Figure 2, Video 2).
evidence: This is stated as the typical workflow and demonstrated in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: Segmentation in MorphoGraphX can be fully automatic or directed by manually placed seeds.
source: The segmentation can be fully automatic (Video 3) or directed by manually placed seeds.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Video 3.

claim: MorphoGraphX allows user-defined Bezier surfaces to interact with volumetric data for visualization and feature extraction.
source: MorphoGraphX allows user-defined surfaces to interact with volumetric data both for visualization and feature extraction. The researcher can interactively define Bezier surfaces to visualize curved slices through an object.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the software.

claim: Bezier surfaces in MorphoGraphX can be converted to a triangular mesh and segmented into cells.
source: The Bezier surface can be converted to a triangular mesh, and segmented into cells with the same procedure used for Figure 2A–E.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the software.

claim: Once a surface is segmented into cells, data collected on a different channel can be projected onto the segmented surface for quantification.
source: Once a surface is segmented into cells, data collected simultaneously on a different channel, such as a GFP fusion to a protein of interest, can then be projected onto the segmented surface (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: MorphoGraphX allows quantification of genetic expression and protein localization at the cellular or sub-cellular scale.
source: This allows the quantification of genetic expression and protein localization at the cellular, or sub-cellular scale.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the software.

claim: Many tools commonly used for the analysis of flat images have been adapted for use on curved surfaces in MorphoGraphX.
source: Many tools commonly used for the analysis of flat images (for example in softwares such as Adobe Photoshop, Gimp and ImageJ) have been adapted for use on curved surfaces in MorphoGraphX. This includes Gaussian blur, erosion, dilation, morphological closing, local minima detection, normalization, etc.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the software.

claim: MorphoGraphX has implemented the watershed transform for cell segmentation on curved surfaces.
source: The flexibility of this approach is demonstrated by our implementation of more complex algorithms, such as the watershed transform for cell segmentation and our adaptation of an algorithm based on signal gradients to compute the orientation of microtubules (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) that was previously implemented in 2D (Boudaoud et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: MorphoGraphX has adapted an algorithm based on signal gradients to compute the orientation of microtubules on curved surfaces.
source: The flexibility of this approach is demonstrated by our implementation of more complex algorithms, such as the watershed transform for cell segmentation and our adaptation of an algorithm based on signal gradients to compute the orientation of microtubules (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) that was previously implemented in 2D (Boudaoud et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and demonstrated in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Signal from different tissue layers can be visualized and quantified in MorphoGraphX by adjusting the depth of projection.
source: Signal coming from different tissue layers can be visualized and quantified by adjusting the depth of projection (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3B–E.

claim: In the shoot apical meristem of Arabidopsis thaliana, PIN1 is first upregulated in the epidermis at the site of incipient primordium initiation before being activated in deeper layers.
source: As an illustration, in the shoot apical meristem of Arabidopsis thaliana we can observe that the auxin efflux carrier PINFORMED1 (PIN1) is first upregulated in the epidermis at the site of incipient primordium initiation before being activated in deeper layers (Bayer et al., 2009; Kierzkowski et al., 2013) (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and demonstrated in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MorphoGraphX can perform quantification at the sub-cellular scale by dividing fluorescence signal into membrane localized and cell interior portions.
source: Quantification can also be performed at the sub-cellular scale (Pound et al., 2012). The amount of fluorescence signal projected onto the triangle mesh can be divided into a membrane localized portion and a cell interior portion (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and demonstrated in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MorphoGraphX is able to process and compare multiple time points.
source: In addition to data from single image stacks, MorphoGraphX is able to process and compare multiple time points.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the software.

claim: MorphoGraphX has developed a user-friendly interface to manually identify cell lineages on curved surfaces representing the tissue at different time points.
source: For this we have developed a user-friendly interface in MorphoGraphX to manually identify cell lineages on curved surfaces representing the tissue at different time points (Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Video 4.

claim: Errors in lineage are detected automatically in MorphoGraphX by comparing the neighborhoods of daughter cells and their parents.
source: Errors in lineage are detected automatically by comparing the neighborhoods of daughter cells and their parents.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the software.

claim: Once co-segmentation is complete in MorphoGraphX, changes in cell area or gene expression over the interval between two time points can be computed and visualized as a heatmap.
source: Once the co-segmentation is complete, changes in cell area or gene expression over the interval between two time points can be computed and visualized as a heatmap (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Cell proliferation can be visualized as a colormap in MorphoGraphX, along with marking of the new walls.
source: Cell proliferation can also be visualized as a colormap (Vlad et al., 2014), along with marking of the new walls (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Pairwise correspondence between time points in MorphoGraphX can be combined in longer time series.
source: Pairwise correspondence between time points can be combined in longer time series (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), for example to perform clonal analysis over several days (Vlad et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: MorphoGraphX can compute the two dimensional Principal Directions of Growth (PDGs) of the surface associated with each cell.
source: The cell junctions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) are used as landmarks to compute the two dimensional Principal Directions of Growth (PDGs) of the surface associated with each cell (Dumais and Kwiatkowska, 2002; Kwiatkowska and Dumais, 2003; Routier-Kierzkowska and Kwiatkowska, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cell lineage information in MorphoGraphX is used to account for cell division and identify only the junctions that are conserved between time points.
source: The cell lineage information is used to account for cell division and identify only the junctions that are conserved in between time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Growth anisotropy in MorphoGraphX is computed from the magnitudes of the growth directions.
source: The growth anisotropy is computed from the magnitudes of the growth directions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MorphoGraphX can calculate local tissue curvature based on the position of the neighbors closer than a given radius.
source: Other directional quantities can also be computed, stored and displayed in MorphoGraphX on a cellular basis. For example, the local tissue curvature (Goldfeather and Interrante, 2004) can be calculated based on the position of the neighbors closer than a given radius and displayed in a manner similar to the growth directions (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), making it a convenient tool for precise staging of fast growing organs such at the shoot apical meristem (Kwiatkowska and Dumais, 2003; Kwiatkowska, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and demonstrated in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The shoot apex is the source of all the aerial structure of the plant.
source: The shoot apex is the source of all the aerial structure of the plant.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: At the summit of the shoot apex, a slow growing central zone harbors the stem cell niche, surrounded by a fast growing peripheral zone where organ initiation occurs.
source: At the summit, a slow growing central zone harbors the stem cell niche, surrounded by a fast growing peripheral zone where organ initiation occurs (Steeves and Sussex, 1989; Dumais and Kwiatkowska, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Similar patterns of growth, cell proliferation and organ geometry were observed in the tomato shoot apex as those reported in other species.
source: We observed similar patterns of growth, cell proliferation and organ geometry in the tomato shoot apex as those reported in other species (Kwiatkowska and Dumais, 2003; Grandjean et al., 2004; Kwiatkowska, 2004; Reddy et al., 2004; Kwiatkowska and Routier-Kierzkowska, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the comparison.

claim: The first geometrical indicator of primordium initiation in the tomato shoot apex was a slightly elevated curvature at the corner of the meristem.
source: The first geometrical indicator of primordium initiation we noted was a slightly elevated curvature at the corner of the meristem (Kwiatkowska and Dumais, 2003; Kwiatkowska, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations to support it.

claim: The early change in shape at the site of primordium initiation coincided with increased growth in the peripheral zone.
source: This early change in shape coincided with increased growth in the peripheral zone.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: The peripheral zone of the tomato shoot apex displayed differential growth dependent on the dynamics of primordium initiation.
source: The peripheral zone itself displayed differential growth dependent on the dynamics of primordium initiation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: Regions adjacent to older primordia in the tomato shoot apex exhibited fast, highly anisotropic expansion.
source: Regions adjacent to older primordia exhibited fast, highly anisotropic expansion (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and demonstrated in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The part of the meristem closest to the newly separated primordium was not distinguishable based on growth rates.
source: In contrast, the part of the meristem closest to the newly separated primordium (P1 in Figure 4) was not distinguishable based on growth rates.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The accelerating growth of the peripheral zone progressively pushed away newly formed organs as they differentiated, making more space available on the meristem for further initiation.
source: As previously observed in Anagallis arvensis (Kwiatkowska and Dumais, 2003; Kwiatkowska and Routier-Kierzkowska, 2009), this accelerating growth of the peripheral zone progressively pushed away newly formed organs as they differentiated, making more space available on the meristem for further initiation and suggesting a possible feedback between lateral organ growth and meristem expansion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations to similar findings in other species.

claim: Auxin activity is already visible at the first sign of primordium initiation in the tomato shoot apex.
source: Interestingly, while auxin activity is already visible at the first sign of primordium initiation, DR5 expression does not strictly correlate with growth.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: DR5 expression does not strictly correlate with growth in the tomato shoot apex.
source: Interestingly, while auxin activity is already visible at the first sign of primordium initiation, DR5 expression does not strictly correlate with growth.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: No DR5 signal is detected in the fast expanding regions close to older primordia in the tomato shoot apex.
source: In particular, no DR5 signal is detected in the fast expanding regions close to older primordia.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: DR5 expression is present in the crease separating young primordia from the meristem, an area where the cells exhibited a slight decrease in surface area.
source: We also found that DR5 expression is present in the crease separating young primordia from the meristem, an area where the cells exhibited a slight decrease in surface area (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and demonstrated in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells in the boundary between primordium and meristem displayed a small increase in length only in the direction parallel to the border, suggesting compression by the growing organ.
source: As shown in previous studies (Kwiatkowska and Dumais, 2003; Kwiatkowska, 2004; Kwiatkowska and Routier-Kierzkowska, 2009), the quantification of growth anisotropy shows that cells in the boundary displayed a small increase in length only in the direction parallel to the border between meristem and primordium, suggesting compression by the growing organ (Hamant et al., 2008) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations and demonstrated in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3.

claim: Volumetric segmentation requires very high quality of signals, since the cell outlines must be visible from all angles.
source: However, volumetric segmentation requires very high quality of signals, since the cell outlines must be visible from all angles.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for 3D segmentation.

claim: For plant tissues, 3D segmentation of cells from confocal images is mainly used in the case of cleared, fixed samples or limited to the outermost layers of cells.
source: For plant tissues, which often display autofluorescence, 3D segmentation of cells from confocal images is therefore mainly used in the case of cleared, fixed samples (Bassel et al., 2014; Yoshida et al., 2014) (Figure 5B–D) or limited to the outermost layers of cells (Figures 5A, 6D).
evidence: This is stated with citations and demonstrated in Figures 5 and 6D.

claim: MorphoGraphX uses the auto-seeded, morphological watershed algorithm available in the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit (ITK) for 3D segmentation.
source: MorphoGraphX uses the auto-seeded, morphological watershed algorithm available in the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit (Yoo et al., 2002) (ITK) for 3D segmentation.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the ITK toolkit.

claim: MorphoGraphX has developed a collection of user-friendly 3D voxel editing tools allowing the researcher to correct segmentation errors.
source: We have developed a collection of user-friendly 3D voxel editing tools allowing the researcher to correct segmentation errors.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the software.

claim: Geometrical properties and fluorescent signal of 3D cells can be quantified in MorphoGraphX.
source: As with 2D surfaces of cells, geometrical properties (surface area, wall length, volume) and fluorescent signal (e.g., total signal per cell, membrane localization) of the 3D cells can be quantified (Figure 5) and exported to spreadsheet files for further analysis (Bassel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: Cells segmented in 3D in MorphoGraphX can be exported for use in simulation models where highly realistic geometries are required.
source: Cells segmented in 3D can also be exported for use in simulation models, where highly realistic geometries are required (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 5D.

claim: Co-segmentation with approximately 30° difference in view angle led to small segmentation differences, averaging to less than 2%.
source: To estimate the error introduced by this effect, we imaged the same sample twice from different angles (Kierzkowski et al., 2012). Co-segmentation with approximately 30° difference in view angle lead to small segmentation differences, averaging to less than 2% (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result and demonstrated in Figure 6A,B.

claim: There is no obvious bias from the view angle in MorphoGraphX segmentation.
source: Note that there is no obvious bias from the view angle.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the validation experiment.

claim: The heat maps of volume increase in 3D show the same areas of slow and fast growth as the surface segmentation.
source: The heat maps of volume increase in 3D show the same areas of slow and fast growth as the surface segmentation.
evidence: This is stated as a validation result.

claim: In cases when the tissue thickness is preserved over growth, tracking cell expansion on the surface is a reasonable approximation for volumetric cell expansion.
source: In cases when the tissue thickness is preserved over growth, as in the epidermal layer of the shoot apex, tracking cell expansion on the surface is therefore a reasonable approximation for volumetric cell expansion (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the validation and demonstrated in Figure 6C,D.

claim: For a tomato shoot apex sample, the auto-segmentation error rate was about 2%, with only 12 cells under-segmented (fused) and 1 cell over-segmented (split) over a total of 576 cells.
source: For a tomato shoot apex sample, the auto-segmentation error rate was about 2%, with only 12 cells under-segmented (fused) and 1 cell over-segmented (split) over a total of 576 cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result and demonstrated in Figure 6E.

claim: Automatic seeding considerably shortens the time needed to segment large samples.
source: Automatic seeding considerably shortens the time needed to segment large samples, such as a Drosophila wing disc (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method and demonstrated in Figure 6F.

claim: The total number of cells in a Drosophila wing disc varied by about 3% between automatic and manual segmentation (6304 autosegmented vs 6510 manually seeded cells).
source: The total number of cells varied by about 3% (6304 autosegmented vs 6510 manually seeded cells).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result.

claim: A key strength of MorphoGraphX is the ability to accurately extract curved surface meshes from 3D volumetric data and perform image processing on the resulting curved (2.5D) surface images.
source: A key strength of our MorphoGraphX software is the ability to accurately extract curved surface meshes from 3D volumetric data and perform image processing on the resulting curved (2.5D) surface images.
evidence: This is stated as a key strength of the software.

claim: The curved surface method in MorphoGraphX has wide application, since many biological processes happen on surfaces.
source: This has wide application, since many biological processes happen on surfaces, and the method has been proven in both animal (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012) and plant (Santuari et al., 2011; Chitwood et al., 2012; Kierzkowski et al., 2012; Nakayama et al., 2012; De Rybel et al., 2013; Kierzkowski et al., 2013; Wabnik et al., 2013; Sampathkumar et al., 2014; Vlad et al., 2014; Yoshida et al., 2014) systems, in embryonic as well as mature tissues.
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to published work using the method.

claim: The curved surface method is especially powerful for time-lapse confocal imaging, where laser exposure has to be kept to a minimum, limiting penetration to the outermost layers of the sample.
source: The method is especially powerful for time-lapse confocal imaging, where laser exposure has to be kept to a minimum, limiting penetration to the outermost layers of the sample.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: MorphoGraphX provides an intuitive and user-friendly interface for the visualization and editing of 3D volumetric data.
source: In addition to curved surface image processing, MorphoGraphX provides an intuitive and user-friendly interface for the visualization and editing of 3D volumetric data, making it possible to digitally remove obstructing objects from the surface of interest, such as the peripodial membrane overlying the Drosophila wing disc (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the software with a citation to published work.

claim: MorphoGraphX has included a range of standard 3D image processing tools, similar to those available in many other softwares.
source: We have also included a range of standard 3D image processing tools, similar to those available in many other softwares (Fernandez et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2010; Sommer et al., 2011; Federici et al., 2012; Mosaliganti et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to other software for comparison.

claim: The modular design of MorphoGraphX allows the integration of existing libraries and the creation of custom processing 'pipelines'.
source: The modular design of MorphoGraphX allows the integration of existing libraries and the creation of custom processing 'pipelines', going from the raw microscopy image to feature extraction and fluorescence quantification.
evidence: This is stated as a design feature of the software.

claim: MorphoGraphX is implemented as a collection of shared libraries, and new libraries can be added or removed without recompiling MorphoGraphX.
source: MorphoGraphX is implemented as a collection of shared libraries, and new libraries can be added or removed without recompiling MorphoGraphX.
evidence: This is stated as a design feature of the software.

claim: The most common operations for 3D visualization, filtering and editing in MorphoGraphX have been written to exploit the massively parallel architecture of modern graphics cards.
source: The most common operations for 3D visualization, filtering and editing have been written to exploit the massively parallel architecture of modern graphics cards, which can have thousands of processing cores.
evidence: This is stated as a design feature of the software.
